runs.answer:
Four useful datasets cover **drought conditions, runoff vulnerability, and irrigated land** in the western United States:

| Dataset | Coverage and period | What it provides |
|---|---|---|
| **[Western Land Data Assimilation System (WLDAS), NASA](https://doi.org/10.5067/ABBHPUIGJH5M)** | Western U.S. and surrounding region; catalog period **January 2, 1979–January 1, 2024**; daily, **0.01° grid** | Modeled soil moisture, snow depth and snow-water equivalent, evapotranspiration, groundwater recharge, and anomalies. A useful starting point for historical drought and water-availability analysis—not direct field measurements. |
| **[Runoff vulnerability to the 2015 western U.S. drought, USGS](https://doi.org/10.5066/F7J67FD2)** | **326 western river basins**, focused on **2015** | Measures assessing streamflow vulnerability to drought. Appropriate for a basin-level drought case study rather than ongoing monitoring. |
| **[LANID: Landsat-based irrigation dataset for CONUS 2018–20, USGS](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9YWR0OJ)** | Conterminous U.S., including the West; annual irrigation maps for **2018–2020** | Identifies irrigated crops. **Metadata caveat:** the description also discusses a monthly **2000–2020** HUC12 irrigation-water-use reanalysis, including evapotranspiration, consumptive use, and effective precipitation. Confirm which files belong to this record before assuming those longer series are included. |
| **[Landsat-derived Rainfed and Irrigated-Cropland Product, L3 V002](https://doi.org/10.5067/Community/LGRIP/LGRIP30_L3.002)** | Currently **conterminous U.S.**, despite “Global” in the title; nominal **2020**, using **2019–2021** imagery; **30 m** | Maps irrigated cropland, rainfed cropland, non-cropland, and water bodies. Useful for locating irrigation, but not measuring irrigation-water volumes. |

**Formats and documentation**
- The cropland product advertises **GeoTIFF** rasters, a [user guide](https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/documents/2087/LGRIP30_User_Guide_v2.pdf), and technical documentation.
- WLDAS provides a [dataset page](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/WLDAS_NOAHMP001_DA1_D1.0/summary) and README; its actual data-file format was not established by the inspected metadata.
- The two USGS records advertise DOI access pages and XML metadata; their underlying data formats remain unverified. No standalone data dictionaries were returned.

**Availability caveat:** All four are cataloged as public. NASA records link to government-works terms; explicit reuse terms were not returned for the two USGS records. Download availability, authentication, file sizes, and schemas have not been verified, and none is directly queryable here.

This is a targeted Data.gov search, not an exhaustive inventory. For studying drought alongside irrigation, WLDAS and the irrigation maps are promising starting points, but their periods, spatial units, and measures must be aligned before comparison.

datasets.title: LANID: Landsat-based irrigation dataset for CONUS 2018-20
datasets.description:
This data release provides a monthly irrigation water use reanalysis for the period 2000-20 for all U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Watershed Boundary Dataset of Subwatersheds (Hydrologic Unit Code 12 [HUC12]) in the conterminous United States (CONUS). Results include reference evapotranspiration (ETo), actual evapotranspiration (ETa), irrigated areas, consumptive use, and effective precipitation for each HUC12. ETo and ETa were estimated using the operational Simplified Surface Energy Balance (SSEBop, Senay and others, 2013; Senay and others, 2020) model executed in the OpenET (Melton and others, 2021) web-based application implemented in Google Earth Engine. Results provided by OpenET/SSEBop were summarized to hydrologic response units (HRUs) in the National Hydrologic Model (NHM; Regan and others, 2019) to estimate consumptive use and effective precipitation on irrigated lands. Irrigated lands for the CONUS were provided by the Landsat-based Irrigation Dataset (LANID; Xie and others, 2019) for each year of the reanalysis period. Consumptive use estimates provided by the NHM were disaggregated to HUC12s using area weighted intersections with HRUs and the relative proportion of irrigated lands in each intersected area.
The Landsat-based Irrigation Dataset (LANID) uses a random-forest machine-learning model with greenness and vegetative indices, climate data, and crop masks to identify irrigated crops (Xie and others, 2021, Xie and Lark, 2021). Separate western US and eastern US methods are used to train and validate the model. Annual LANID maps for 2018 -20 were created using the same techniques in Xie and others, 2021, and Xie and Lark, 2021.

datasets.title: Landsat-derived Global Rainfed and Irrigated-Cropland Product L3 2020 30 m V002
datasets.description:
The Landsat-derived Global Rainfed and Irrigated-Cropland Product Level 3 2020 (LGRIP30_L3) Version 2 data provides high-resolution, 30 meter (m) cropland data to assist and address food and water security issues of the twenty-first century. As an extension of the Global Food Security-support Analysis Data ([GFSAD](https://www.usgs.gov/centers/western-geographic-science-center/science/global-food-security-support-analysis-data-30-m)) project, LGRIP L3 V2 maps agricultural croplands by dividing them into irrigated and rainfed croplands, and calculates irrigated and rainfed areas across the globe. LGRIP data are produced using Landsat 8 time-series satellite sensor data for the 2019 through 2021 time period to create a nominal 2020 product.  

Each LGRIP30 L3 V2 30 m resolution GeoTIFF file contains a layer that identifies areas of rainfed cropland (cropland areas that are purely dependent on direct precipitation without any artificial watering), irrigated cropland (cropland that had at least one irrigation during the crop growing period), non-cropland, and water bodies over a 10° by 10° area, as well as an accuracy assessment of the product. A low-resolution browse image is also included.  

Currently, LGRIP30 V2 products only contain data for the conterminous United States (CONUS). LGRIP30 V2 data covering the rest of the globe will be added at a later date.

datasets.title: WLDAS Noah-MP 3.6 Land Surface Model L4 Daily 0.01 degree x 0.01 degree Version D1.0 (WLDAS_NOAHMP001_DA1) at GES DISC
datasets.description: The Western Land Data Assimilation System (WLDAS), developed at Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) and funded by the NASA Western Water Applications Office, provides water managers and stakeholders in the western United States with a long-term record of near-surface hydrology for use in drought assessment and water resources planning. WLDAS leverages advanced capabilities in land surface modeling and data assimilation to furnish a system that is customized for stakeholders’ needs in the region. WLDAS uses NASA’s Land Information System (LIS) to configure and drive the Noah Multiparameterization (Noah-MP) Land Surface Model (LSM) version 3.6 to simulate land surface states and fluxes. WLDAS uses meteorological observables from the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS-2) including precipitation, incoming shortwave and longwave radiation, near surface air temperature, humidity, wind speed, and surface pressure along with parameters such as vegetation class, soil texture, and elevation as inputs to a model that simulates land surface energy and water budget processes. Outputs of the model include soil moisture, snow depth and snow water equivalent, evapotranspiration, soil temperature, as well as derived quantities such as groundwater recharge and anomalies of the state variables.

runs.answer:
**The verified data show changes in climate conditions and agricultural practices, but they do not establish a correlation between them.** That is a limitation of the available evidence—not evidence that no relationship exists.

### What the historical observations show

| Measure | Geography and period | Verified observations |
|---|---|---|
| Annual average temperature | Maryland, 1985–2012 | 54.8°F in 1985 and 57.5°F in 2012—a **2.7°F endpoint increase** |
| Annual precipitation | Maryland, 1985–2012 | Substantial year-to-year variation: for example, 35.79 inches in 1991 versus 60.74 inches in 2003 |
| Estimated cover-crop area | Chesapeake Bay watershed, 2002 and 2012 | Increased from **481.5 to 1,770.6 km²** |
| Estimated conservation-tillage area | Watershed, 1985, 1992, 2002 and 2012 | Fell from **8,077.0 km²** in 1985 to **7,057.3 km²** in 1992, then rose to **8,403.1 km²** in 2012 |

Sources: NOAA NCEI’s Maryland [temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/18/tavg/12/12/1985-2012.csv) and [precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/18/pcp/12/12/1985-2012.csv) series, catalog **C00005**; USGS/Chesapeake Bay Program agricultural estimates, DOI **[10.5066/P9SRZS8P](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9SRZS8P)**.

### Why this does not demonstrate correlation

- **Geographies differ:** Maryland statewide climate does not represent the entire Chesapeake watershed.
- **Practice observations are sparse:** cover crops have only two observation years; conservation tillage has four.
- **Endpoint changes are not trend estimates.** Annual weather fluctuations also should not be mistaken for a long-term climate trend.
- Agricultural areas are **spatially allocated estimates of reported practices**, not adoption rates or direct measurements everywhere. Practices can overlap, so their areas should not be added.
- The practices were reported for soil and water-quality management; these records do not establish climate-driven adoption.

Consequently, reporting a correlation coefficient from these series would be misleading. These are historical snapshots ending in 2012, not current conditions.

### More directly relevant evidence

A targeted catalog search also found USGS studies combining climate, stream conditions and management gradients: **30 agricultural-region streams in Pennsylvania/Maryland during March–September 2023** ([DOI 10.5066/P13EMSZU](https://doi.org/10.5066/P13EMSZU)), plus a **2024 Developed Piedmont study** ([DOI 10.5066/P14XBLPB](https://doi.org/10.5066/P14XBLPB)). These could inform local relationships, but are not long-term adoption studies. Their catalog routes advertise XML metadata; underlying file schemas, dictionaries and detailed use terms remain unverified, and they are not currently queryable here.

**Bottom line:** testing the relationship requires repeated climate and practice observations for matching locations and years. Establishing *why* practices changed would additionally require evidence separating climate influences from policy, incentives and other management drivers.

datasets.title: Stream stage, stream temperature, and climate metrics for 30 streams spanning land use and management gradients in a mixed agricultural region in Pennsylvania and Maryland, 2023
datasets.description:
This data release contains summary metrics describing stream stage, stream water temperature, and short-term climate conditions (daily precipitation and air temperature) for 30 streams spanning gradients of forest and  agricultural land uses and the implementation of agricultural best management practices in a mixed agricultural region in Pennsylvania and Maryland, USA. This setting is the third of four settings or "typologies" that will be assessed for the USGS Chesapeake Stream Team project. High-frequency stage, water temperature, and air temperature (15-minute data) were measured by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from March 2023 to September 2023 and are available at Davis and others (2025; DOI: https://doi.org/10.5066/P13EOQCX). Additional daily air temperature and precipitation data were acquired from the Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) climate data website. Air temperature and water temperature data were used to compute stream water temperature metrics describing stream temperature conditions in each stream during the monitoring period. Stream stage and precipitation data were used to derive stream stage metrics describing stage conditions (a surrogate for flow) for each stream during the monitoring period. Precipitation and air temperature data from PRISM were also used to compute air temperature metrics and precipitation metrics describing climate conditions during the monitoring period. The metrics include:
Air temperature metrics 
- Mean daily minimum, mean, and maximum air temperature
Precipitation metrics 
- Total precipitation depth
- Maximum daily precipitation depth
- Average precipitation depth per days with precipitation
- Frequency of precipitation days
Stream stage metrics
- Number of runoff events
- Frequency of runoff events 
- Standard deviation in unit-value stage
Stream water temperature metrics
- Coefficient of variation of mean and maximum daily water temperatures
- Number of days with temperatures of 20 or 25 degrees Celsius or greater
- Duration of time above 20 or 25 degrees Celsius or greater
- Maximum of seven-day moving average of daily maximum temperature and daily mean temperature
- Mean of daily minimum, mean, maximum, and daily water temperature range
- A thermal sensitivity metric, which is the slope estimate from linear regression model of mean daily water temperature versus mean d

runs.answer:
Estimated cover-crop implementation in the Chesapeake Bay watershed **increased by 1,289.06 km² between 2002 and 2012**, a rise of approximately **268%**—about **3.68 times** the 2002 area.

| Year | Estimated cover-crop area |
|---|---:|
| 2002 | 481.51 km² |
| 2012 | 1,770.57 km² |

These are spatially allocated estimates based on reported practices, summed across watershed catchments—not direct measurements at every location or farmer adoption rates. Only the two observation years are available, so the figures do not show the year-by-year trajectory.

**Source:** USGS / Chesapeake Bay Program, `covcrop.csv`, [DOI: 10.5066/P9SRZS8P](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9SRZS8P).  
Reproducibility evidence ID: `0815de313baa4e6db48e571048c32a76`.
